proposedFields.title: Water Across the Carved Sign
proposedFields.summary: Use flowing water across a reusable inscribed tile as a temporary ritual carrier, then return both water and tile to ordinary use without ingestion or health claims.
proposedFields.intro: Cippi of Horus combine carved images, inscribed protective speech, and water passed over the surface. The cited Brooklyn Museum object belongs to this ancient Egyptian tradition; it is not Wiccan and the exact inscribed passage still requires independent verification. This modern adaptation retains contact between water and a marked surface while replacing medical use with a brief, non-ingestible Wiccan reflection on carrying an intention into action.

proposedFields.body:
1. Choose one ordinary quality you want to carry into a specific action today, such as patience during a conversation or steadiness while completing a task. Write the quality and action in your notebook. Avoid health, emergency, or guaranteed-result intentions.

2. On a clean, unglazed ceramic tile, draw one simple personal mark with a washable pencil. The mark must be your own; do not copy a museum image or claim it is an Egyptian sign. Place the tile in a shallow basin beside a sink.

3. Pour a small amount of plain tap water slowly across the tile while saying, “Water crosses the sign; my chosen action carries on.” This is original modern wording. The water’s contact with the marked surface is the historical technique retained here.

4. Watch the mark darken or soften for one breath. Name aloud the practical action written in your notebook. Do not describe the water as medicine, poison treatment, or a substance with guaranteed power.

5. Lift the tile and let excess water return to the basin. Set it on a towel. Pour the used water directly down the sink; send it directly to the drain; it is not a beverage, stored preparation, spray, or topical material.

6. Wash the tile with ordinary soap, rinse it, and dry it completely. Erase the temporary mark. Returning the object to ordinary use closes the working and distinguishes a temporary ritual tool from a permanent historical replica.

7. Complete the named action within the time you chose. Later, record whether the water-contact sequence helped you remember the commitment. Judge the practice by attention and follow-through rather than by a supernatural outcome.

proposedFields.title: Seven-Knot Household Guardian
proposedFields.summary: Tie a seven-knot cord for a safe household location while replacing the source’s child-worn amulet with a non-wearable modern boundary marker.
proposedFields.intro: Berlin Papyrus 3027 preserves a dawn protective text and directs that a seal and hand emblem be made into a protective object tied with seven knots, one knot in the morning and another in the evening until seven are complete. The historical object was connected with protecting a child. This is ancient Egyptian household magic, not Wicca. The modern adaptation retains the seven-knot sequence and alternating daily timing while placing the cord high on a household hook, never on a child or body.
proposedFields.introduction: Berlin Papyrus 3027 preserves a dawn protective text and directs that a seal and hand emblem be made into a protective object tied with seven knots, one knot in the morning and another in the evening until seven are complete. The modern adaptation retains the seven-knot sequence and alternating daily timing while placing the cord high on a household hook, never on a child or body.
proposedFields.body:
1. Choose a short length of thick cotton cord in a visible color. Select a high indoor hook or closed storage place that children and pets cannot reach. The cord will mark a household boundary; it must never be worn, tied to furniture that may tip, or placed across a doorway.

2. Write one concrete household care commitment, such as checking door locks, storing medicine securely, or keeping an exit clear. The commitment is modern and practical. It replaces the historical claim that an amulet repels harmful dead or disease.

3. On the first morning, hold the loose cord and say, “This home is tended through watchful care.” Tie one loose overhand knot near an end. This wording is original and does not translate the papyrus.

4. That evening, review the care commitment and complete one small related action. Tie a second knot. Continue morning and evening, tying only one knot at each session, until the seventh knot is complete. The alternating sequence follows Erman’s description; the safety actions are modern additions.

5. Keep every knot loose enough to inspect. As you tie, avoid naming another person as a threat or promising supernatural protection. Each knot records attention already given or an action you freely undertake.

6. After the seventh knot, count all seven once. Say, “Seven knots complete the sign; protection continues through the care that is mine.” Hang the cord at the selected inaccessible indoor location.

7. Record the seven care actions in a notebook. Inspect the cord monthly for fraying, then retire it after one season by cutting it into short pieces before disposal. Replace it only when beginning seven new, specific household actions.

proposedFields.title: The Red-Heading Ritual Plan
proposedFields.summary: Write a practical ritual plan with visually separated preparation, action, and closure headings, following the handbook character of an Egyptian magical-medical manuscript.
proposedFields.intro: The London Medical Papyrus is a working compilation of incantations and recipes rather than scripture. Wreszinski’s public-domain edition describes red headings and instructions used to separate operations, although the exact passage supporting this seed record still needs review. This modern Wiccan lesson retains the practical handbook principle: a working is written as an ordered procedure that can be checked before it begins.

proposedFields.body:
1. Select one harmless, self-directed ritual you already understand, such as arranging a reflective bowl, placing a stone beside a journal, or making a silent altar dedication. Do not choose food preparation, bodily application, combustion, or a medical purpose for this planning exercise.

2. Divide one page into four sections. Write the headings “Purpose,” “Preparation,” “Action,” and “Closure” in red pencil. Use black pencil for all instructions. The two-color system is a modern visual adaptation inspired by manuscript rubrics; it is not a copied Egyptian layout.

3. Under Purpose, write one sentence about what the working helps you practice. Under Preparation, list every object and the exact place it will be used. Remove anything unnecessary or hazardous.

4. Under Action, write three to seven numbered steps. Begin each step with a verb. Include a stopping time and keep every action under your control. If a step depends on another person, record their consent or rewrite the step.

5. Under Closure, state how every material returns to ordinary use, storage, recycling, or disposal. Add one observable next action so the ritual does not end with an unsupported promise.

6. Read the complete page aloud once. Say, “Written with order, performed with care, completed and closed.” This is original modern wording. Correct missing tools, unclear quantities, or a closure that cannot be completed.

7. Perform the plan exactly once or store it for later review. Afterward, mark each completed section and note any instruction that failed in practice. Revise the handbook entry rather than inventing an explanation or claiming a supernatural certainty.

proposedFields.title: The Standing Image and Flowing Water
proposedFields.summary: Create a temporary upright image beside flowing water to practice the historical relationship among image, recitation, and liquid without imitating treatment.
proposedFields.intro: Ancient Egyptian healing statues and cippi joined an upright inscribed image with spoken text and water. The seed cites a healing statue and the Brooklyn Museum cippus, but its exact passages and translation rights remain under review. This modern Wiccan adaptation studies the relationship through an original paper image standing beside—not inside—water, separating it from the direct-contact tile practice taught elsewhere.

1. Fold a sheet of heavy paper into a freestanding card. On its face, draw an original image of yourself standing calmly. Add three small symbols representing resources you can actually use, such as a phone, door, book, friend, or path.

2. Place the card upright on a dry counter at least a hand’s width from the sink. Set a clear bowl in the sink below the tap. The historical image-and-water relationship inspires this arrangement; no ancient figure or inscription is copied.

3. Read the three resources aloud. Then say, “Image before me, water below; I remember the help I already know.” This is original modern wording and assigns no healing function to the image or water.

4. Run a thin stream of plain water into the bowl for three breaths while looking at the standing card. Name one situation in which you will use one listed resource. Keep the paper dry and the bowl inside the sink.

5. Turn off the tap. Pour the bowl out immediately and set it upside down to drain. Send the water directly to the drain; it is not a beverage, stored preparation, spray, or material for bodily application. The working concerns symbolic relationship, not preparation of a potion.

6. Fold the card closed so the image is no longer visible. Write the chosen resource and next action on the outside. This visible-to-hidden change marks the end of the ritual gaze and the start of ordinary follow-through.

7. Dry the sink area, return the bowl, and place the folded card in your notebook. Complete the next action. Recycle the card when the action is finished rather than preserving it as a medical or guaranteed protective object.

proposedFields.title: Naming the Act Before the Altar
proposedFields.summary: Name a ritual action precisely before beginning it, using an altar card to distinguish the practitioner, the method, and the hoped-for purpose.
proposedFields.intro: The Metternich Stela gives Heka a divine role within protective speech, but the seed’s exact section and reusable translation remain unapproved. 1. Choose one small ritual action that is harmless and entirely yours, such as placing a stone beside a journal, opening a window briefly, or arranging a clean cloth. Decide what skill it represents: attention, courage, rest, or another grounded quality.

2. On a card, complete three lines: “I am the practitioner.” “My action is ___.” “My purpose is to practice ___.” Avoid titles of authority, promises of results, and claims that an ancient deity speaks through you.

3. Put the card on a clean altar or table with the single tool required for the action. Leave all unrelated objects off the surface. Read the card aloud at an ordinary volume.

4. Say, “Named is the actor, named is the deed, named is the purpose I choose to feed.” This is original modern wording. Pause and check that the deed still matches the purpose. If it does not, revise the card before proceeding.

5. Perform the action once. Describe it in literal language as you do it: “I place the stone,” “I open the window,” or “I unfold the cloth.” Do not turn the description into a prediction or command aimed at another person.

6. Return the tool to its ordinary state. Beneath the three lines, write what physically happened and one next action that supports the named quality. Cross out any outcome that was outside your control.

7. Close by saying, “The act is finished; the purpose continues through my choices.” Store or recycle the card. Use a new card for a different act so the name, method, and purpose remain specific rather than becoming a generic affirmation.

proposedFields.title: The Protective Encircling Gesture
proposedFields.summary: Use a four-part self-encircling gesture to name personal boundaries, resources, exit, and consent without claiming an ancient Isis rite.
proposedFields.intro: The seed cites protective speeches associated with Isis and the Metternich Stela, including the image of divine protection surrounding Horus. The exact passages and translation rights remain pending, and this is ancient Egyptian religion rather than Wicca. The modern adaptation uses the documented theme of encircling protection as a self-directed Wiccan boundary exercise, without reenacting healing claims or speaking as Isis.

proposedFields.body:
1. Stand or sit in a clear area with enough room to extend one hand. Place a small card and pen within reach. Choose one situation in which you need a boundary governing your own participation, not control over another person.

2. Face forward and touch your hand lightly to your chest or hold it nearby. Say, “At the center, I name my consent.” Write what you freely agree to do and what you do not agree to do.

3. Gesture slowly to your right and say, “At this side, I name my resources.” List one person, policy, tool, or place you can genuinely contact. Gesture to your left and say, “At this side, I name my limits.” State one clear limit.

4. Gesture behind you without twisting beyond comfort and say, “Behind me, an exit remains.” Identify how you can pause, leave, decline, or ask for help. The four-part movement is a modern structure inspired by surrounding protection; it is not recorded as an Isis gesture.

5. Trace one comfortable open arc in front of you, leaving a visible gap rather than closing a rigid circle. Say, “Care may surround me; my way remains open.” This is original modern wording.

6. Read the consent, resource, limit, and exit once. Choose one practical step, such as sending a message, adjusting a plan, or moving an object. Do not interpret bodily sensations as prophecy.

7. Lower your hand, step out through the imagined gap, and complete the chosen step. Tear up the card if privacy requires. The open exit and ordinary action complete the working; repeated circling is unnecessary.

proposedFields.title: The Sealed Botanical Method Card
proposedFields.summary: Pair one sealed botanical token with a written ritual method, keeping symbolic speech separate from evidence-based care.
proposedFields.intro: The London Medical Papyrus places spoken charms and material recipes in the same working collection. Its precise usable passage remains pending, and no ancient remedy is reproduced here. 1. Choose one intact dried culinary bay leaf from your own kitchen supply. Seal it inside a small transparent pouch without crushing it. The leaf is a modern symbolic token; the pending source record does not establish bay as an ancient correspondence for this lesson.

3. Beneath those headings, add “Ordinary support.” Record one evidence-based action appropriate to your situation, such as keeping an appointment, following written professional guidance, resting, or asking a qualified person a question. Do not write a diagnosis or alter prescribed care.

4. Put the sealed leaf and card on a clean table. Speak the sentence once, then point to each of the three sections in order: material, words, ordinary support. This deliberate separation is the central modern exercise.

5. Spend five minutes beginning the ordinary action if possible. The botanical token does not cause the result; it marks the ritual portion of the plan while the written action preserves practical accountability.

6. Say, “Symbol is symbol, care is care; I close the rite with both made clear.” Put the sealed leaf away from food preparation areas so it is not accidentally used.

7. Review the card later. Record what the ritual helped you remember and what required ordinary support. Discard the leaf pouch intact after one use, keeping it away from children and pets.

1. Draw a simple human outline on a large sheet of paper. It need not resemble you. Mark ten numbered points from top to bottom: head, eyes, nose, upper arms, lower arms, chest, middle, thighs, shins, and feet.

2. Set ten flat paper tokens beside the outline. Choose one practical care word for each point, such as rest, clarity, air, strength, skill, breath, nourishment, movement, balance, and grounding. These words are modern and are not ancient correspondences.

3. Beginning at the head, place one token at each numbered point. Speak the body-area name and its care word. Keep the sequence in order so no point is skipped; complete coverage is the historical structural idea retained here.

4. After the fifth point, pause and check your breathing and posture. Continue only if comfortable. The exercise is attention and symbolism, not examination, diagnosis, or treatment.

5. At the feet, say, “Named from crown to ground, each part receives attention; the whole remains my own.” This is original modern wording. Look over the complete map once.

6. Choose one care word that can become an ordinary action today. Write the action beside the outline, such as taking a scheduled break or arranging suitable support. Do not infer a problem from the map.

7. Remove the tokens from feet to head, count them, and store them. Fold or recycle the outline. The reverse removal closes the sequence and prevents the paper figure from being treated as a permanent proxy for yourself or anyone else.

proposedFields.title: The Words-and-Actions Ledger
proposedFields.summary: Plan one bounded ritual by recording its spoken words separately from its physical actions, then reunite them in a safe sequence.
proposedFields.intro: The Maqlu corpus preserves incantations across eight tablets and a ninth ritual tablet that orders their accompanying actions. The ritual tablet repeatedly pairs an incantation opening with a material instruction. This is ancient Mesopotamian anti-witchcraft practice, not Wicca. The modern adaptation keeps the documented discipline of coordinating speech and action while omitting figurines, accusations, sulphur, fire, and claims of supernatural attack.

proposedFields.body:
1. Choose one self-directed purpose that can be addressed symbolically, such as ending a period of rumination or preparing to begin a task. Set a fifteen-minute limit. On a clean sheet, draw two columns titled “Words” and “Actions.” This two-column format is modern; its inspiration is the source’s separation and coordination of incantation and ritual instructions.

2. In the Actions column, write three safe movements: arrange one ordinary object, pause for three breaths, and return the object to its usual place. Use a stone, cup, or key that already belongs to you. Do not use a weapon, flame, smoke, bodily material, or an image of another person.

3. Beside each movement, write one short sentence in the Words column. Make every sentence describe your own choice. Avoid commands aimed at another person and avoid promising a result. The source contains hostile accusations; this adaptation expressly removes them.

4. Read the ledger silently from top to bottom. Check that every spoken line has one clear action and that the final action restores the space. Revise any vague instruction before starting.

5. Perform the first action and speak its paired sentence once. Continue down the page without adding spontaneous threats, ingredients, or repetitions. If the sequence stops feeling appropriate, end it and proceed to cleanup.

6. After the third pair, say, “The words are spoken; the actions are done; this working is closed.” This is original modern wording. Put the object away and take three ordinary breaths.

7. Mark each completed pair with a check. Record whether the written order made the practice clearer. Keep the ledger as a planning record, or recycle it if it contains private thoughts. Do not repeat the working merely to force certainty.

proposedFields.intro: Maqlu Ritual Tablet line 6′ directs the recitation of the incantation identified by its opening “I call upon you” three times. Later fragmentary instructions again preserve a threefold recitation. The ancient rite proceeds into hazardous burning and hostile imagery. This modern Wiccan adaptation retains only the attested use of a fixed threefold recitation to structure speech. It supplies new wording, a firm stopping point, and no claim that repetition compels a being or outcome.

proposedFields.body:
1. Choose one thought or habit you want to set down for the next part of the day. Phrase it as your own action, such as “I release this task until tomorrow,” rather than a demand directed at another person.

2. Place three flat counters in a row on a stable table. Set a five-minute timer. The three counters are a modern counting aid; the source records a threefold recitation but does not prescribe these objects.

3. Write one sentence of no more than twelve words. Read it once and check that it contains no prediction, accusation, medical claim, or attempt to control someone. If it does, rewrite it as a boundary governing your own conduct.

4. Touch the first counter and speak the sentence at an ordinary volume. Take one unforced breath. Touch the second counter and repeat the same words without intensifying them. Breathe again, then touch the third and make the final repetition.

5. After the third recitation, turn all three counters face down or move them into a small group. Do not add a fourth repetition. The fixed ending is part of the modern safety boundary and distinguishes deliberate ritual repetition from compulsive checking.

6. Say, “Three times spoken, now complete; I return to the choice before my feet.” This is original modern wording. Write one practical next action that matches the boundary you stated.

7. Put the counters away and carry out that action if it remains safe and useful. Record how the first, second, and third repetitions felt different. Wait until another day before using the method for a different issue.

entries.proposedConcept: A bedside protection working adapted from a specific dream passage

proposedFields.title: The Waking Dream Fold
proposedFields.summary: Close a frightening dream through orientation, a folded written record, and a firm return to the waking room.
proposedFields.intro: The cited Chester Beatty dream spells combine recitation with bread, beer-steeped herbs, myrrh, and contact with the face after waking. Their exact passages and translation rights remain pending. This modern Wiccan adaptation retains an immediate spoken response and a physical completion sequence but omits every historical substance and makes no claim to explain, prevent, or medically treat dreams.

proposedFields.body:
1. Prepare before sleep by placing a notebook, pencil, and small empty envelope beside the bed. Keep the walking path clear. Write today’s date on the envelope, then leave it open.

2. If a frightening dream wakes you, first orient to the room. Name the date if known, the place, and three ordinary things you can see. Turn on a gentle light if needed. Do not begin divination while disoriented.

3. Write no more than five factual details from the dream. Avoid deciding what it predicts or what another person secretly intends. Beneath the details write, “This was a dream; interpretation can wait.”

4. Fold the note once and place it in the envelope. Say, “The dream is recorded and bounded; waking choice returns to me.” This is original modern wording, replacing the source’s substances and formula.

5. Close the envelope and place it in a drawer or closed box. Feel both feet or hands supported by the bed or floor and take three unforced breaths. Do not repeatedly reopen the note during the night.

6. Choose a quiet waking action: adjust the room temperature, take a normal sip from your usual bedside beverage, or contact a trusted person if appropriate. No ritual ingredient is prepared or consumed.

7. Review the note in daylight only if useful. Record one emotion and one ordinary support action, then recycle or retain it privately. If nightmares are frequent, severe, trauma-related, or impair sleep, seek qualified health support rather than relying on the ritual.

entries.proposedConcept: A symbolic support charm with no medical or pregnancy claim

proposedFields.title: Two Tiles of Welcomed Support
proposedFields.summary: Prepare two symbolic altar tiles and name two consent-based forms of practical support for a birth or another welcomed transition.
proposedFields.intro: Berlin Papyrus 3027 includes a birth-related recitation spoken over two bricks associated with the birthing place. Erman’s 1901 edition also records fine linen, offerings, incense, and fire. This is ancient Egyptian ritual material, not Wicca. The modern adaptation retains two marked supports, linen, spoken care, and protective intention while removing physical use of birth bricks, combustion, animal offerings, and claims about labor or health.

proposedFields.body:
1. Choose a transition you are personally undergoing or supporting with consent: pregnancy, recovery after birth, adoption, beginning a caregiving role, or another clearly named act of bringing something into life. Write the person’s chosen name or the transition’s title on a card. Do not use this ritual to predict or manage a medical outcome.

2. Place two flat ceramic tiles side by side on a stable altar or table. The source speaks over two birth bricks; these tiles are symbolic altar objects only. No person should stand, sit, kneel, or labor on them.

3. Lay a small piece of clean linen across the tiles. Erman’s passage names fine linen clothing for the officiant. This adaptation moves linen onto the altar and removes specialist dress, meat and bird offerings, incense, and fire.

4. Set the card on the linen. If the named person is someone other than you, confirm that they welcome this spiritual support. Say, “May care surround this passage; may choice, skill, and compassion meet it.” This is original modern wording.

5. Name two forms of practical support—one for each tile. Examples include preparing a meal, arranging transport, respecting rest, or following an agreed contact plan. Write only actions that the recipient has requested or accepted.

6. Fold the linen once over the card without tying it. Say, “The rite is closed; the promised care remains.” Leave the folded linen on the tiles for the duration of one quiet breath, then remove it. The two supports you named, rather than the objects, carry the commitment forward.

7. Return the tiles to ordinary storage. Give or perform the promised support at the agreed time. Store the card privately or recycle it. If pregnancy or birth is involved, follow the recipient’s clinical care plan and contact qualified maternity or emergency services when needed.

proposedFields.title: The Riverbank Boundary Card
proposedFields.summary: Create a dry boundary card that distinguishes water, shoreline, and human path while studying an animal-danger papyrus without reenacting it.
proposedFields.intro: The Harris Magical Papyrus groups hymns and incantations concerning crocodiles and other dangerous animals. The surviving manuscript is incomplete, and this seed record does not identify one approved operational passage. Rather than inventing a crocodile spell, this modern Wiccan lesson uses the documented danger-at-water context to create a dry symbolic boundary paired with ordinary water-safety decisions.

proposedFields.body:
1. On a blue sheet of paper draw one horizontal line to represent water. On a brown or plain sheet draw a second line to represent shore. Place the sheets edge to edge on a dry table, never beside actual open water.

2. Cut a small arrow from scrap paper to represent the human path. Place it on the shore side. The colors and arrow are modern teaching tools, not copied Egyptian symbols or correspondences.

3. Write three water-safety boundaries beside the path: use designated access, obey posted warnings, and keep distance from wildlife. Add one boundary appropriate to your region or planned activity.

4. Say, “Water has its realm, wildlife has its way, and I keep to the path of care.” This is original modern wording. Move the arrow along the shore without crossing the drawn waterline.

5. Name one historical fact documented by the seed: the papyrus organizes material concerning crocodiles and other dangerous animals. Then name what remains unknown: the exact action and words of the selected passage. This prevents the symbolic exercise from being presented as a reconstruction.

6. Fold the water sheet away from the path and place the arrow on your written safety list. The physical separation marks closure. Do not leave paper outdoors or use the card as a real warning marker.

7. Store the list with travel or outdoor plans if relevant. Before visiting water, consult current local guidance, weather, closures, and wildlife notices. The ordinary decision governs conduct; the paper ritual does not create protection.

entries.proposedConcept: A seven-point ritual boundary adapted from an attested vessel-divination arrangement

proposedFields.title: The Seven-Point Boundary
proposedFields.summary: Arrange seven ordinary objects to define a temporary, self-directed space for reflection, then dismantle it deliberately.
proposedFields.intro: The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden uses repeated groups of seven in a vessel-divination preparation: seven bricks or palm sticks, seven clean loaves, seven lumps of salt, seven recitations, and a seventh-hour limit. This is Roman-period Egyptian ritual practice, not ancient Wicca. The modern adaptation keeps the documented use of seven to structure space and repetition while removing the child medium, oil divination, food, spirit invocation, and supernatural claims.
proposedFields.introduction: The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden uses repeated groups of seven in a vessel-divination preparation: seven bricks or palm sticks, seven clean loaves, seven lumps of salt, seven recitations, and a seventh-hour limit. This is Roman-period Egyptian ritual practice, not ancient Wicca. The modern adaptation keeps the documented use of seven to structure space and repetition while removing the child medium, oil divination, food, spirit invocation, and supernatural claims.
proposedFields.body:
1. Choose a stable table or clear floor area where seven small objects cannot become a trip hazard. Select seven matching stones, wooden disks, or coasters. Do not use food, salt, flame, oil, or stacked bricks. Write one question about your own conduct or priorities and set a seven-minute timer.

2. Clean the surface and place the first object at the point nearest you. Arrange the other six clockwise until they form a loose ring with an open center. Count aloud as each object is set down. The count comes from the source; the ring and clockwise direction are modern construction choices.

3. Place your written question in the center. Say, “Seven points mark the time and place; my judgment remains my own.” This is original modern wording, not a translation of the papyrus.

4. Take seven unforced breaths. On each breath, name one fact, uncertainty, resource, limit, possible action, consequence, or next step connected to the question. If one category has no answer, say “unknown” rather than inventing certainty.

5. Spend the remaining time writing. Keep observations separate from interpretations, and do not treat a thought, image, or coincidence as a guaranteed message. Stop when the timer sounds even if the answer feels incomplete.

6. Read the next step you recorded. If it is safe, lawful, and within your control, schedule it. Otherwise revise it into a smaller action. The practical action, rather than a promised omen, carries the work forward.

7. Remove the objects one at a time in reverse order while counting down to one. Fold the question, put the objects away, and restore the surface to ordinary use. Deliberate dismantling completes the boundary and prevents repeated checking for a preferred answer.

proposedFields.title: The First-Person Threshold
proposedFields.summary: Speak one original first-person statement while crossing from reflection into an ordinary chosen action.
proposedFields.intro: Maqlu Ritual Tablet line 23′ identifies an incantation by the first-person opening “I have been sent and I will go,” then pairs it with arranged figurines. The historical procedure belongs to Mesopotamian anti-witchcraft ritual and does not document Wicca. This adaptation retains first-person ritual speech and purposeful movement while removing figurines representing accused people, burning, divine compulsion, and claims of attack.

The historical procedure belongs to Mesopotamian anti-witchcraft ritual and does not document Wicca. This adaptation retains first-person ritual speech and purposeful movement while removing figurines representing accused people, burning, divine compulsion, and claims of attack.
proposedFields.body:
1. Identify one ordinary action you have freely chosen and can safely begin now: making a necessary call, opening a work document, tidying one surface, or taking a brief walk. Write the action in plain language.

2. Choose a doorway or another visible threshold in your own space. Clear the floor on both sides. Place a single flat marker beside the threshold, never where it could cause a trip. The marker and doorway are modern substitutions; the source’s first-person line is paired with arranged figurines, which this version excludes.

3. Stand on the starting side and name what is true: “I have chosen my next action.” Then name the action. Do not claim that a deity, omen, or another person ordered it.

4. Say, “I set my direction, and I go by my own consent.” This is original modern wording, not a translation. Step across the threshold once. If mobility makes stepping unsuitable, move the marker from one side of a line on the table to the other.

5. Pause after crossing and take one unforced breath. Begin the chosen action for at least two minutes. The practical beginning is essential; the spoken threshold is not presented as sufficient by itself.

6. When the two minutes end, decide whether to continue, schedule the remainder, or stop. Each option remains yours. Avoid repeating the crossing to seek a feeling of certainty.

7. Return the marker to storage and restore the walkway. Write one sentence beginning “I chose” and one beginning “I did.” These statements keep personal agency visible and close the working without assigning power to the threshold itself.

proposedFields.title: Boundary, Removal, Washing
proposedFields.summary: Complete a three-part closing sequence that marks a boundary, removes one temporary symbol, and finishes with ordinary handwashing.
proposedFields.intro: Near the close of the Maqlu ritual tablet, the procedure moves through a drawn boundary around a bed, removal of the fire in the morning, and a series of handwashings at dawn. 1. At the end of an evening reflection, write one concern you will not continue working on tonight. Use a sentence about your own attention. Do not identify another person as a magical threat.

2. Lay four flat coasters around the notebook to mark its temporary boundary. The source draws a circle around a bed; four coasters are a modern, removable substitute that avoids powders on floors and keeps exits clear.

3. Spend five minutes recording what is known, what is uncertain, and the next time you will address the concern. When the timer ends, close the notebook. Say, “The boundary is held; tonight’s inquiry is complete.” These are original modern words.

4. Gather the coasters and carry the closed notebook to its normal storage place. The source removes ritual fire in the morning; this smoke-free and flameless action retains removal as a distinct stage without reproducing combustion or disposal in a river.

5. Go to a sink and wash your hands with ordinary soap and comfortably warm water. Treat this as normal hygiene that also marks the change of activity. Make no claim that water removes illness, curses, or another person’s influence.

6. Dry your hands, return the towel, and turn off the light in the work area. Say, “What is closed may rest; morning will meet what remains.” Do not reopen the notebook that night merely to repeat the sequence.

7. At the next appropriate time, review only the practical action you recorded. Complete, revise, or discard it using ordinary judgment. The three movements are a structure for closure, not a prediction or promise about what follows.

proposedFields.title: The Scribe’s Authority Check
proposedFields.summary: Write and test one ritual statement in your own voice, distinguishing learned competence from borrowed divine authority.
proposedFields.intro: The Metternich Stela presents Thoth as a specialist in protective speech, and some Egyptian formulas let a practitioner speak from a divine identity. The exact reusable passage remains unapproved. Modern Wicca does not grant ancient Egyptian priestly authority. This adaptation keeps writing, skilled speech, and review while requiring the practitioner to speak only from personal knowledge and responsibility.
proposedFields.introduction: The Metternich Stela presents Thoth as a specialist in protective speech, and some Egyptian formulas let a practitioner speak from a divine identity. The exact reusable passage remains unapproved. Modern Wicca does not grant ancient Egyptian priestly authority. proposedFields.body:
1. Choose one ritual statement you intend to use in a self-directed working. Write it at the top of a page. Underline every claim about identity, knowledge, authority, or outcome.

2. Make three columns titled “I know,” “I choose,” and “I cannot claim.” Sort each underlined phrase into one column. Move references to another person’s thoughts, future certainty, ancient office, or divine identity into “I cannot claim.”

3. Rewrite the statement using only “I know” and “I choose.” For example, replace “I command certainty” with “I choose to examine what I know.” This is an ethical editing method, not a translation of a Thoth formula.

4. Place a pen horizontally beneath the revised text as a boundary. Say, “Skill is practiced, words are reviewed, and authority stays with what I can answer for.” This is original modern wording.

5. Read the revised statement once. Check whether it gives a physical instruction, a clear ending, and room for uncertainty. If it does not, revise it again before using it.

6. Perform only the harmless, self-directed action named in the statement. Return the pen to ordinary use and draw a closing line beneath the entry.

7. Record what evidence would cause you to change the statement. Keep the page as a versioned ritual note or recycle it. Never speak as an ancient deity, claim a historical office, or use ritual authority to override another person’s consent or professional advice. Date the final version so later revisions remain visible rather than being presented as timeless authority.

3. Move the lower stone slightly toward the center and name one action already taken. Move the upper stone toward the center and name one piece of planning still useful. Continue alternating until you have made seven total movements.

4. Count every movement aloud. The number seven comes from the seed’s claimed historical instruction; moving stones and the planning/action meanings are modern substitutions for a knotted application at the foot.

5. When the stones meet near the center, say, “What is above can guide; what is below can move; neither stands alone.” This is original modern wording.

7. Put the stones away and complete the next action if appropriate. Do not place stones on the body, tie anything to a foot, or use the layout for pain, injury, illness, or other health concerns. Record whether the alternating layout changed your plan, then close the notebook before beginning another question.

proposedFields.title: Dawn Water Closure
proposedFields.summary: Use ordinary handwashing at dawn or the start of the day to close a difficult period of reflection without reproducing the source’s burning rites.
proposedFields.intro: The Maqlu ritual tablet moves from destructive fire symbolism to quenching, sprinkling, repeated washing, and dawn formulas. This is ancient Mesopotamian ritual, not Wicca. 7. Open a curtain or step into ordinary daylight if safe, then complete the chosen action. Repeat the practice on another day only for a newly defined reflection, not as a compulsive attempt to force certainty.

proposedFields.intro: The seed contrasts the wedjat eye, associated with restoration and used by living and dead, with the heart scarab’s funerary role in judgment. 1. Choose two visibly different, ordinary stones. Wash and dry them before the ritual if needed. Designate one “Recovery” and the other “Judgment” on two paper labels; do not carve, paint, or copy a wedjat or scarab image.

2. Place Recovery on the left label. Write one difficulty from which you are already rebuilding and one resource that supports that process. Avoid promises that the stone heals or restores anything by itself.

proposedFields.title: The Circle Around the Vessel
proposedFields.summary: Mark a temporary protective boundary around a reflective bowl, conduct one short inquiry, and erase the boundary completely.
proposedFields.intro: Maqlu Ritual Tablet lines 19′–22′ pair water sprinkling with a circle drawn around a crucible using gypsum and roasted flour. The surrounding rite is Mesopotamian anti-witchcraft practice, not Wicca, and later actions include hazardous fire and hostile figurines. This modern adaptation retains the attested techniques of water, a vessel, and a visible encircling boundary while substituting a dry bowl and a removable paper circle.
proposedFields.introduction: Maqlu Ritual Tablet lines 19′–22′ pair water sprinkling with a circle drawn around a crucible using gypsum and roasted flour. The surrounding rite is Mesopotamian anti-witchcraft practice, not Wicca, and later actions include hazardous fire and hostile figurines. This modern adaptation retains the attested techniques of water, a vessel, and a visible encircling boundary while substituting a dry bowl and a removable paper circle.
proposedFields.body:
1. Place a dry, unbreakable bowl on a stable table away from edges and electrical equipment. Set a ten-minute timer. Write one question about your own boundaries or responsibilities on a separate card.

2. Put a large sheet of paper beneath the bowl. Draw one complete circle on the paper around the bowl without moving the vessel. The source uses gypsum and roasted flour around a crucible; paper and pencil are modern substitutions that avoid loose powder and do not reproduce the source’s fire setting.

3. Place the question card beside the bowl, outside the circle. Say, “This line marks the work I choose to hold; what lies beyond it remains beyond my claim.” This is original modern wording.

4. Look at the empty center and list three matters that belong within your control. Then list three matters outside your control. Do not use the boundary to claim ownership of another person’s choices or to diagnose a supernatural attack.

5. Move only the items within your control onto the question card. Choose one achievable next action. The bowl remains empty; it serves as the documented vessel form without holding a preparation, flame, or substance.

6. When the timer ends, lift the bowl and erase the pencil circle completely. If erasing is impractical, fold the paper inward until the line is hidden and recycle it. Say, “The marked space is released; my responsibility is clear.”

7. Return the bowl to ordinary use and complete or schedule the chosen action. Store the card only if useful. Do not preserve the circle as a permanent ward or repeat the inquiry to compel reassurance.

proposedFields.title: The Seven-Factor Talisman Record
proposedFields.summary: Dedicate an ordinary object by documenting seven meaning-bearing factors while labeling every modern choice.
proposedFields.intro: The seed’s museum essay describes seven contributors to an Egyptian amulet’s force: shape, decoration, inscription, color, material, spoken words, and actions. This is a secondary summary and does not yet satisfy the primary-passage requirement. The modern lesson uses those seven analytical factors as a transparent dedication record, without claiming the object becomes an Egyptian amulet or borrowing ancient color meanings.

proposedFields.body:
1. Choose one ordinary object you already own, such as a smooth token, key ring, or plain pendant that will not be worn during the exercise. Clean it according to its normal care instructions and place it on a stable table.

2. Number a page from one to seven. Record the object’s shape, decoration, inscription, color, and material in the first five lines. Describe only what is physically present; do not assign an ancient meaning.

3. On line six, write one original sentence you will speak over the object. On line seven, write one harmless action you will perform with it, such as placing it beside a task list while beginning work.

4. Review all seven lines. Mark each interpretation as “modern personal association.” Remove any claim that a color, material, or symbol had a documented Egyptian meaning unless an approved passage later supports it.

5. Speak the line-six sentence once: “Seven factors named with honest care; this object recalls the work I choose to share.” This is original modern wording.

6. Perform the line-seven action, then write the observable result. The object acts as a reminder within the practice; it does not compel an outcome or acquire verified historical power.

7. Store the object normally and keep the seven-factor record with your notes. If you change its use, create a new record rather than pretending the original dedication covers every purpose. Do not sell or present it as an authentic Egyptian amulet. Date the record and note where the ordinary object is stored after the working closes.
